title: How to Take Yourself on a Solo Coffee Shop Date: What to Pack and What to Do
dek: Pack the bag, pick the place, order well and choose from six things to do once you're settled: a notebook, a book, a pocket sketch set.

body.text: A window seat, a good drink and an hour that is entirely yours. A coffee shop may be the easiest place in town to sit by yourself. It's built for it: laptops, paperbacks, one-person tables, nobody asking questions, and you can leave whenever you like. The usual hurdle is a small, silly worry that people will wonder why you're alone. They're mostly looking at their own phones.
A small bag does most of the work. Something to read, something to write with and a tote you can keep on your lap are enough for a first hour, and a few extras make the next one even nicer.

essentials: A book, notebook or sketchbook (something that lets you look down comfortably)
Headphones, if you like a soundtrack
A small tote or bag you can keep on your lap or at your feet
optional: A light cardigan, since cafes can be chilly
A phone charger, but only if you're staying more than an hour
A small bookmark or sticky tabs for marking pages or passages

body.text: **What makes it easier:** a pocket notebook, a book sleeve and a reading journal, so your bag feels date-ready and your hands have something lovely to do.

body.title: Pack the date
body.dek: A pocket notebook, a book sleeve and a journal make your bag feel date-ready and give your hands something lovely to do.

body.text: Step 2: Pick the right kind of place
Decide what you want from the hour first.

items: **Quiet and calm** if you want to read or write. Look for softer music, a few armchairs and people who are mostly alone.
**Lively and bright** if you want to people-watch and feel part of a scene. Larger windows and bar seating are your friends.
**Close to home** if you're nervous. Familiar streets lower the stakes, and a walk home afterward feels like a bonus.

body.text: Go at a quieter time for your first outing: a mid-morning or mid-afternoon weekday visit often means easier seat choices and less pressure.
Step 3: Order like you mean it

Treat the order as part of the date. Choose something you wouldn't make at home, like a proper pot of tea or the pastry you keep eyeing. Many cafes offer decaf, herbal tea and milk alternatives, so you can match the drink to the time of day. If you have an allergy or dietary need, ask the staff directly about ingredients rather than guessing. Think of your order as your ticket to a seat for the hour.
Step 4: Choose a seat with an escape hatch

Window seats and counter seats are the friendliest for one: you have something to look at and you're not facing a room. If the cafe is busy, a small table or a counter stool is considerate and feels less exposed.

Many cafes are happy for you to sit with a book or notebook, but busy ones may need tables back at peak times. A good rule: buy something, don't spread out over a big table at the lunch rush, and reorder if you're settling in for a while. If in doubt, ask or watch what other people do. Keep your bag with you, and don't leave a laptop or phone unattended if you step away.
The awkwardness tends to peak around minute five, when you realize nobody is looking at you and nobody is going to rescue you either. The fix is cheerfully practical: give yourself a job.

steps: Take one slow sip and look around for three things you like: a mug, a plant, someone's boots.
Open your book or notebook and read or write one full page.
If your mind wanders, write down what it wandered to.
After thirty minutes, decide whether to order a second drink or head out.

body.text: Six things to do once you're settled

items: **Read one chapter.** Set a timer for twenty minutes if you need to protect it from your phone. **What makes it easier:** a book sleeve, so a paperback travels safely in your tote.
**Write three pages.** Journal, morning-pages-style or just a list of what you want this month. **What makes it easier:** a notebook with pages you like writing on, so the blank page feels inviting.

**Sketch the room.** Draw the lamp, the cup, someone's hands (without staring). **What makes it easier:** a tiny [watercolor](/journal/watercolor-painting-for-beginners) set and a small sketch pad, which make this feel fancy and fit in a coat pocket.
**Make a plan for the weekend.** Write down three things you could do and circle one. **What makes it easier:** a pocket notebook, so the plan lives in your bag.

**Write a letter or postcard.** The cafe is a good place to finally answer a friend. **What makes it easier:** a small letter-writing set with a few cards and envelopes, so you can post it on the way home.
**Do absolutely nothing.** Watch the street. It counts, and it's harder than it sounds.

body.title: For the sketch-and-letter hour
body.dek: A pocket watercolor set, a small sketch pad and a letter-writing set turn a spare hour at the table into something you can hold at the end.

items: **Shorten the date.** Thirty minutes counts. A good ending is better than a long slog.
**Change seats.** A different angle can change the whole feeling.
**Take the drink to go.** Walk it to a bench or the park and make the second half of the date outdoors.
**Try again somewhere else.** If one cafe doesn't suit you, it's not a verdict on solo dates.

body.text: Once the first one goes well, repeat it. A regular slot, like Saturday at ten or Wednesday after work, and two or three cafes to rotate between, is easier to protect than a one-off. A line in a notebook after each visit (the chapter, the sketch, the idea that surfaced) gives you a small record of how it went.
Pick the cafe, pick the hour and save the date. Make Some Plans can hold your Saturday at ten.

When you're ready for something bigger, browse [30 solo date ideas](/journal/solo-date-ideas), or build a whole day with [how to plan a solo Saturday](/journal/how-to-plan-a-solo-saturday). If the page-and-pen part appeals, [junk journaling](/journal/how-to-start-junk-journaling) is a good next step, and so is [a reading journal](/journal/how-to-start-a-reading-journal) if you would rather keep notes on what you read.
